Radisson Mining released new drill results from its Quebec-based O’Brien gold project. 
The drill highlights: 
52.34 g/t gold over 3.0m, including 154.95 g/t over 1.0m
66.93 g/t gold over 1.0m
10.62 g/t gold over 4.7m, including 40.90 g/t over 1.1m
These latest six drill results added to the total drill program at this previously unexplored 800 meter zone between two proven mineralization areas have resulted in an 82% hit-rate that’s consistent with Radisson’s resource model. 
That’s good news because it validates the likelihood that the mineralization may bridge the two other zones - turning into one large trend. 
The ongoing drilling in this area is a part of a 140,000 meter, 8 drill rig step-out project, entirely focused on adding to the resource story. 
Currently, O’Brien has Indicated resources of 0.63 Moz (5.59 g/t Au) + Inferred 1.69 Moz (5.08 g/t Au). 
Radisson’s July 2025 Preliminary Economic Assessment estimated an 11-year mine life with low capex. 
In August 2026, Agnico Eagle invested $41 million to help Radisson fund an underground exploration program. 
What’s next: Radisson continues to drill and explore, working towards an updated resource estimate.

text:
RE: Mako Mining Exploits Royalty Valuation Arbitrage via Sailfish Stream

You guys might find this transaction interesting.

Mako Mining just announced a 20-year gold stream with Sailfish Royalty valued at roughly $403.2 million—essentially a left-hand to right-hand transaction by Wexford Capital, since they control both sides. Instead of cash, Mako agrees to sell gold to Sailfish at just 25% of spot. In exchange, Mako gets 70 million new Sailfish shares—roughly a 49% ownership stake.

The whole play exploits a valuation arbitrage where royalty companies command massive multiple premiums over traditional mining operators. Sailfish is trading at a much higher multiple, and its accumulation of physical gold ounces will create massive leverage to a rising gold price. Simultaneously, Mako's equity position in Sailfish could benefit from unrealized paper gains until they decide to sell.

Personally, I hate these forms of financial engineering, but it's smart. I wonder if management cooks up another transaction when their two development projects become fully bolstered mines, or if the stronger balance sheets of Sailfish and Wexford will allow Mako to perform a large acquisition. If shares sell off from geopolitical noise, I might add a bit of both.
